questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[Dev] Choose all the correct statements about the waterfall process:

options.text: Each phase must be completed before the next phase begins
options.explanation: True. Phases are strictly sequential; each one is signed off before the next starts.

options.text: Testing is performed throughout all phases of development
options.explanation: False. Testing is a separate phase near the end; continuous testing belongs to agile/XP.

options.text: It may produce software customers do not want
options.explanation: True. The customer sees working software only at the end, so misunderstood or changed needs are found too late.

options.text: It is suitable for projects with clear, well-understood, and stable requirements
options.explanation: True. With stable requirements little rework is needed, so the up-front plan works.

questions.explanation: Waterfall is a plan-driven, sequential process: requirements, design, implementation, testing, operation, one after the other.

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[Dev] Agile vs. waterfall

options.text: Waterfall process is iterative
options.explanation: False. Waterfall is linear and sequential, not iterative.

options.text: Agile is about following a well-defined plan
options.explanation: False. That describes plan-driven processes; agile prefers responding to change.

options.text: Agile emphasizes comprehensive requirement documents
options.explanation: False. Agile prefers working software over comprehensive documentation.

options.text: Agile can be both iterative and incremental
options.explanation: True. Agile builds the product in small increments, refined over repeated iterations (sprints).

options.text: You must implement Scrum to be agile
options.explanation: False. Scrum is one agile framework; XP, Kanban and others are also agile.

questions.explanation: Agile values responding to change over following a plan and working software over comprehensive documentation (Agile Manifesto).

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[Dev] Choose the correct statement about Scrum:

options.text: Each sprint aims to complete a few backlog items
options.explanation: True. The sprint backlog holds the few items the team commits to finishing in that sprint.

options.text: Product owner must be the project manager
options.explanation: False. The product owner represents the customer and owns the backlog; they should not be the project manager.

options.text: The Scrum master is the only person allowed to assign tasks to team members during a sprint
options.explanation: False. The team self-organises and members pick tasks; the Scrum master is a facilitator, not a task assigner.

options.text: Scrum focuses on contract negotiation
options.explanation: False. Agile values customer collaboration over contract negotiation.

options.text: Scrum mandates a strict step-by-step software process
options.explanation: False. Scrum is a lightweight framework, not a strict step-by-step process.

questions.explanation: Scrum is a lightweight framework: a self-organising team delivers a few product backlog items in each time-boxed sprint.

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[Dev] Choose the correct statements about XP:

options.text: Pair programming: two programmers working together to write code
options.explanation: True. Pair programming is two developers at one workstation writing the same code.

options.text: XP is a part of the Scrum process
options.explanation: False. XP is a separate agile method; teams may combine XP practices with Scrum, but it is not part of Scrum.

options.text: Code review is the study of source code by the original authors
options.explanation: False. Code review is done by people other than the author.

options.text: TDD aims to write tests before writing actual code
options.explanation: True. In TDD you write a failing test first, then the code to pass it.

questions.explanation: Extreme Programming (XP) is an agile method built on engineering practices such as pair programming, TDD, code review and continuous integration.

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[Ops] What are some of the tasks in software operations?

options.text: Install software on cloud servers
options.explanation: True. Installing and deploying software on servers is an operations task.

options.text: Ensure that certain coding standards are followed properly
options.explanation: False. Coding standards are a development concern (code review, linters).

options.text: Monitor server infrastructure and network traffic
options.explanation: True. Monitoring infrastructure and traffic is core operations work.

options.text: Respond to unplanned service interruptions
options.explanation: True. Incident response to outages is operations work.

options.text: Conduct data analysis to improve availability and performance
options.explanation: True. Analysing monitoring data to improve availability and performance is operations work.

options.text: Defense against personal attacks on top management
options.explanation: False. Not a software operations task (distractor).

questions.explanation: Operations keeps the software running for users: deployment, monitoring, incident response and performance/availability analysis.

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[Ops] What do we measure in monitoring:

options.text: Response time
options.explanation: True. Response time (latency) shows user-facing performance.

options.text: Downtime
options.explanation: True. Downtime measures availability.

options.text: CPU utilization
options.explanation: True. CPU utilisation shows resource load.

options.text: The number of senior managers
options.explanation: False. Headcount of managers is not a system metric.

options.text: Network traffic coming to your servers
options.explanation: True. Incoming network traffic shows load and possible attacks.

options.text: All of the above
options.explanation: False. Option d is wrong, so "all of the above" is wrong.

questions.explanation: Monitoring measures technical health metrics of the running system: latency, availability, resource use and traffic.

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[Ops] What are the problems with Dev and Ops silos?

options.text: We can deploy to production every few minutes
options.explanation: False. Frequent deployment is a benefit of DevOps, not a problem of silos.

options.text: Deployments are isolated activities done after code-build
options.explanation: True. Deployment becomes a separate, late step instead of part of the pipeline.

options.text: Differences in delivery timelines
options.explanation: True. Dev (fast sprints) and Ops (stability, change windows) work on different timelines.

options.text: Creating "throw it over the wall" handoffs that slow delivery and reduce operability
options.explanation: True. Dev "throws" code to Ops, who did not help build it, slowing delivery and making it harder to run.

questions.explanation: When Dev and Ops work as separate silos, software is handed over late, teams work to different timelines and deployments are slow and painful.

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[DevOps] What is DevOps about?

options.text: Close collaborations between software developers and operations engineers
options.explanation: True. DevOps is close collaboration between developers and operations engineers.

options.text: Operation tasks are considered together with development tasks
options.explanation: True. Operational concerns are planned with development work.

options.text: The use of automation to build/test/deploy software and infrastructure
options.explanation: True. Automated build, test and deployment (CI/CD, infrastructure as code) is central to DevOps.

options.text: The separation of two different teams doing agile and devops respectively
options.explanation: False. A separate "agile team" plus "DevOps team" is the DevOps anti-pattern; it recreates the silos.

options.text: Providing support for the whole software lifecycle
options.explanation: True. A DevOps team supports software from design to production operation.

questions.explanation: DevOps breaks the Dev/Ops silo: one team, shared responsibility and automation across the whole lifecycle.

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

[DevOps] Choose the correct statements:

options.text: DevSecOps only considers security at the end of the dev process
options.explanation: False. DevSecOps integrates security throughout the process, not at the end.

options.text: DevSecOps only considers security at the end of the ops process
options.explanation: False. Same reason: security is continuous, not an end-of-ops gate.

options.text: It can be challenging for operations personnel to understand software design problems
options.explanation: True. Ops staff were not involved in design, so design problems are hard for them to diagnose.

options.text: "Shift left" means doing more dev work at the early stages of a software project
options.explanation: False. "Shift left" means doing security and testing earlier, not more dev work.

options.text: Creating a dedicated DevOps team always eliminates silos between development and operations
options.explanation: False. A separate DevOps team is an anti-pattern that can reinforce silos.

questions.explanation: DevSecOps builds security into every stage instead of a gate at the end; "shift left" moves security and testing earlier.

questions.stem:
*Week 1 - Software Processes*

How does the "DevOps anti-pattern" of assigning a separate "DevOps team" reinforce silos?
questions.modelAnswer:
A separate "DevOps team" is just the old operations team with a new name. The agile development team still builds the software and hands it over for the DevOps team to deploy and operate.
This keeps the "throw it over the wall" handoff, split responsibilities and different goals, which are the silos DevOps aims to break down. Real DevOps puts dev and ops skills in one team that designs, tests, deploys and runs its own features.
questions.explanation: The slides name this the DevOps anti-pattern: calling an ops team a "DevOps team" next to an agile dev team, which hands the software over to be operated.

questions.stem:
*Week 2 - User Stories, Estimation, Planning*

[Week 1 Review] Choose the correct statements:

options.text: In a waterfall process, the phases are not followed in order
options.explanation: False. Waterfall phases are strictly in order.

options.text: Iterative and incremental processes can't accommodate changes
options.explanation: False. Iterative and incremental processes exist to accommodate change.

options.text: Agile emphasizes contract negotiation over customer collaboration
options.explanation: False. Agile values customer collaboration over contract negotiation.

options.text: In Scrum, product owner should not be the project manager
options.explanation: True. The product owner represents the customer and backlog; combining it with project manager is discouraged.

options.text: Monitoring server infrastructure and supporting users are part of software operations
options.explanation: True. Monitoring and user support are operations tasks.

options.text: With Dev and Ops silos, we can deploy to production every few minutes
options.explanation: False. Silos slow deployment; frequent deploys come from DevOps.

options.text: In DevSecOps, "shift left" means doing more dev work during the early stages of a software project
options.explanation: False. "Shift left" means moving security and testing earlier.

options.text: In DevSecOps, it is good to have a Dev team and a separate SecOps team
options.explanation: False. A separate SecOps team is a silo; security should be inside the DevOps team (DevSecOps).

questions.explanation: Review of Week 1: waterfall, agile, Scrum roles, operations and DevSecOps.

questions.stem:
*Week 2 - User Stories, Estimation, Planning*

Select all the incorrect statements regarding software requirements:

options.text: Business should dictate all decisions to keep projects on schedule
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Business and developers decide together; business alone cannot judge technical cost.

options.text: Technical jargon improves shared understanding with business stakeholders
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Jargon hurts shared understanding; user stories use the user's language.

options.text: Changing requirements and complexity hinder accurate estimates
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: Changing requirements and complexity do make estimates hard.

options.text: We should make incremental decisions using early and frequent feedback
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: Incremental decisions with frequent feedback is the agile approach.

questions.explanation: The question asks for the incorrect statements. Requirements need shared understanding between business and developers.

questions.stem:
*Week 2 - User Stories, Estimation, Planning*

The project is about building a web app for job seekers. Which of the following can be considered good user stories?

options.text: Charting will be done with Python
options.explanation: False. A technology choice, not user value.

options.text: Recruiter wants to export matched job data to an Excel file
options.explanation: True. One user role, one valuable and testable feature.

options.text: As a user, I want the website to be amazing so I can enjoy using it
options.explanation: False. "Amazing" is vague and not testable.

options.text: The system should prompt users to save their work every 5 mins
options.explanation: True. A specific, testable feature that gives users value.

options.text: As a recruiter and a job seeker, I want to upload resumes, download job postings, send automatic emails, and set reminders so that I can use the system fully
options.explanation: False. Too big (an epic) and mixes two roles; it must be split.

options.text: The software will be released by Nov 30
options.explanation: False. A release date is a plan or constraint, not a feature.

questions.explanation: A good story describes one valuable, testable feature from a user's view (INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable).

questions.stem:
*Week 2 - User Stories, Estimation, Planning*

Adding details to user story - choose the correct statements:

options.text: All details need to be provided far in advance
options.explanation: False. Details are added when the story is about to be implemented.

options.text: Some details can be missing when implementation starts
options.explanation: True. Remaining details are worked out in conversation during implementation.

options.text: Details given far in advance are usually accurate
options.explanation: False. Early details often become wrong as understanding and requirements change.

options.text: Providing all details in advanced is costly
options.explanation: True. Writing details that later change or get dropped wastes effort.

questions.explanation: Details are added just in time, through conversation, because needs change and early detail is wasted.

questions.stem:
*Week 2 - User Stories, Estimation, Planning*

What are the 3Cs for a user story?

options.text: Cash-Car-Condo
options.explanation: Wrong. A joke distractor.

options.text: Customer-Conversation-Creation
options.explanation: Wrong. "Customer" and "Creation" are not the 3Cs.

options.text: Card-Conversation-Confirmation
options.explanation: Correct. Card, Conversation, Confirmation.

options.text: Client-Construction-Confirmation
options.explanation: Wrong. "Client" and "Construction" are not the 3Cs.

questions.explanation: Ron Jeffries' 3Cs: a short Card, the Conversation that adds details, and the Confirmation (acceptance criteria) that shows the story is done.

questions.stem:
*Week 2 - User Stories, Estimation, Planning*

Why user stories?

options.text: Developers like to read requirement documents
options.explanation: False. Stories exist to replace long requirement documents.

options.text: They can be understood by both users and developers
options.explanation: True. Plain-language stories give users and developers a shared understanding.

options.text: They emphasize written communications
options.explanation: False. They emphasise verbal communication (the Conversation), not written documents.

options.text: They encourage detailed requirement very early in the project
options.explanation: False. They defer details until just before implementation.

questions.explanation: User stories are short, in plain user language, and push teams to talk instead of writing long specs.

questions.stem:
*Week 2 - User Stories, Estimation, Planning*

Choose the correct statements regarding story point estimation:

options.text: You can confidently give a story 40 points
options.explanation: False. A 40-point story is too large to estimate confidently; split it.

options.text: We need fine-grained, precise estimation scale
options.explanation: False. Use a coarse scale (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13); precision is false accuracy.

options.text: We should just use hours, not points
options.explanation: False. Points measure relative size and complexity, independent of who does the work.

options.text: We should estimate as a team
options.explanation: True. Team estimation pools knowledge and builds shared understanding.

options.text: We can only estimate story points in a sprint
options.explanation: False. Stories are estimated during backlog refinement and release planning too.

options.text: Each story should be estimated on its own
options.explanation: False. Stories are estimated relative to each other (compared with a reference story).

questions.explanation: Story points are relative size estimates, made by the whole team (e.g. planning poker) on a coarse scale.

questions.stem:
*Week 2 - User Stories, Estimation, Planning*

For a sprint:

options.text: Longer duration is better
options.explanation: False. Short sprints give faster feedback.

options.text: Should complete some stories in the backlog
options.explanation: True. Each sprint delivers some completed backlog stories.

options.text: Product owner decides which stories to do
options.explanation: False. The product owner prioritises, but the team decides what it can commit to.

options.text: Burndown line has to be straight
options.explanation: False. A burndown chart is rarely a straight line; it shows real progress.

options.text: Sprint backlog records all user stories for the project
options.explanation: False. The sprint backlog holds only this sprint's items; the product backlog holds all stories.

options.text: We can estimate tasks in hours
options.explanation: True. In sprint planning, stories are broken into tasks estimated in hours.

questions.explanation: A sprint is a short, fixed time-box (typically 2-4 weeks) in which the team completes a few backlog stories, broken into tasks estimated in hours.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Version control concepts: choose the correct statements

options.text: It is a good idea to use Dropbox for collaborative coding
options.explanation: False. File sync has no history, branches or merge support, and overwrites changes.

options.text: There is no need for version control when you work alone
options.explanation: False. Alone you still need history, undo and branches.

options.text: All repositories can have the same role in distributed versioning
options.explanation: True. In a distributed VCS every repository is a full peer; "central" is just a convention.

options.text: In Git, you can do version control without network connection
options.explanation: True. Commits, branches and history are local; only push/pull need the network.

options.text: It is not possible to have a central repo in Git
options.explanation: False. Teams usually agree on a central repo (e.g. on GitHub).

options.text: Git uses delta-based version control
options.explanation: False. Git stores snapshots, not deltas.

questions.explanation: Git is a distributed VCS: every clone is a full repository, so most work is local.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Git - recording changes:

![Git file lifecycle: Untracked, Unmodified, Modified, Staged. Arrows: add the file (Untracked to Staged), edit the file (Unmodified to Modified), stage the file (Modified to Staged), remove the file (Unmodified to Untracked), commit (Staged to Unmodified)](images/q0021-wooclap-w3-q3-file-lifecycle.png)

options.text: Commit adds files into the staging area
options.explanation: False. `git add` stages files; commit saves the staged snapshot into the repository.

options.text: .git folder contains all files in the working directory
options.explanation: False. `.git` holds the repository database (objects, refs), not the working files.

options.text: Untracked files can't be staged
options.explanation: False. "Add the file" moves an untracked file straight to Staged.

options.text: None of the above
options.explanation: True. a, b and c are all wrong.

questions.explanation: In the diagram, `git add` moves files to Staged and `git commit` records the staged snapshot in the repository.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

About commits:

![Commit graph: master and HEAD point to caf2ca, which has two parents 1a410e and 1f44cd; both have parent cac0ca; cac0ca has parent 1fd4dc (first commit)](images/q0022-wooclap-w3-q4-commit-graph.png)

options.text: They all live in the working directory
options.explanation: False. Commits live in the repository (`.git`), not the working directory.

options.text: Three commits can share a parent
options.explanation: True. Any number of branches can start from one commit; in the picture cac0ca already has two children.

options.text: Each commit only has a single parent
options.explanation: False. Merge commit caf2ca has two parents; the first commit has none.

options.text: None of the above
options.explanation: False. Option b is correct.

questions.explanation: Commits form a graph: a commit can have many children (branches) and more than one parent (merges).

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Object graph of Git:

![Git object graph: commits 1fd4dc, cac0ca and 1a410e each point to a tree; trees point to blobs "version 1", "new file" and "version 2"; the new.txt blob fa49b0 is shared by the second and third commits' trees](images/q0023-wooclap-w3-q5-object-graph.png)

options.text: Each version of a file is stored only once
options.explanation: True. A blob is keyed by its content hash; one version is stored once.

options.text: The blob stores pointers to parent commit
options.explanation: False. A blob holds only file content; the commit points to its parent.

options.text: Multiple commits can share the same copy of a file
options.explanation: True. Blob fa49b0 ("new file") is shared by the second and third commits.

options.text: The tree node stores actual file content
options.explanation: False. A tree holds file names and pointers to blobs; blobs hold content.

options.text: A commit object stores a pointer to its parent
options.explanation: True. Each commit points to its parent commit(s) and its tree.

questions.explanation: Commit → tree → blobs. Objects are named by their content hash, so identical content is stored once.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Git - undoing changes:

options.text: "git revert" erases commit history
options.explanation: False. `git revert` adds a new commit that undoes an old one; history is kept.

options.text: "git checkout <file>" discards uncommitted changes in <file>
options.explanation: True. It restores the file from the last commit, losing uncommitted edits.

options.text: Deleting .git folder has no effect on git operations
options.explanation: False. Deleting `.git` deletes the whole repository and history.

options.text: All are correct
options.explanation: False. Only b is correct.

questions.explanation: Git can undo at different levels; `revert` is the safe, history-keeping way.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Git branching:

options.text: A Git branch is a copy of the git repository
options.explanation: False. A branch is a pointer, not a copy, which is why branching is cheap.

options.text: A pointer to any commit can be a branch
options.explanation: True. A branch is a named pointer to a commit.

options.text: HEAD can point to any of the branches
options.explanation: True. HEAD marks the checked-out branch and moves on `git checkout`/`git switch`.

options.text: "git checkout <branch>" commits changes to <branch>
options.explanation: False. It switches branches; it does not commit.

options.text: "git branch <name>" creates the new commit <name>
options.explanation: False. It creates a new branch pointer, not a commit.

questions.explanation: A branch is a lightweight movable pointer to a commit; HEAD points to the current branch.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Git merging:

options.text: A fast-forward merge moves the commit forward
options.explanation: False. The branch pointer moves forward; commits do not move.

options.text: A fast-forward merge creates a new commit
options.explanation: False. Fast-forward creates no new commit.

options.text: A three-way merge needs a common ancestor
options.explanation: True. It compares both tips with their common ancestor (the three "ways").

options.text: A three-way merge creates no new commit
options.explanation: False. A three-way merge creates a merge commit with two parents.

questions.explanation: Fast-forward: the target is a direct ancestor, so the branch pointer just moves. Three-way: histories diverged, so Git merges the two tips with their common ancestor into a new merge commit.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

What kind of merging is this?

![Commit graph: C0, C1, C2, then C4 on master and C3, C5 on iss53; C6 has parents C4 and C5; master points to C6, iss53 points to C5](images/q0027-wooclap-w3-q9-merge.png)

options.text: Fast-forward
options.explanation: Wrong. A fast-forward makes no merge commit; here C6 has two parents.

options.text: Three-way
options.explanation: Correct. Merging two diverged branches using common ancestor C2 makes merge commit C6.

options.text: No merging
options.explanation: Wrong. C6 is a merge commit.

options.text: Branching
options.explanation: Wrong. The picture shows branches being joined, not created.

questions.explanation: The histories diverged at C2 (C4 on master, C3-C5 on iss53). Merge commit C6 has two parents, C4 and C5.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Remote repository:

options.text: All your branches are visible on the remote server
options.explanation: False. Only branches you push are on the remote; local branches stay private.

options.text: "git pull": send all your changes to the remote server
options.explanation: False. `git pull` downloads and merges; `git push` sends.

options.text: There can be conflicts when pushing to a remote server
options.explanation: True. A push is rejected if the remote has new commits; you must pull and resolve conflicts first.

options.text: None of the above
options.explanation: False. Option c is correct.

questions.explanation: Remotes only receive what you push; pull fetches and merges remote changes into your branch.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Choose the correct statements:

![Two boxes: (1) a repository with commits 0b743, a6b4c, f4265 and branch master; arrow "git clone janedoe@git.ourcompany.com:project.git"; (2) a repository with the same commits, origin/master and a local master both on f4265](images/q0029-wooclap-w3-q11-clone.png)

options.text: The local computer is shown in part (1)
options.explanation: False. Part (1) is the remote server being cloned from.

options.text: The remote git server is shown in part (2)
options.explanation: False. Part (2) is the local computer after `git clone`.

options.text: There is no remote git server
options.explanation: False. git.ourcompany.com is the remote server.

options.text: None of the above
options.explanation: True. a, b and c are all wrong.

questions.explanation: Part (1) is the remote server (git.ourcompany.com). Part (2) is the local clone, which has the remote-tracking branch `origin/master` and its own `master`.

questions.stem:
*Week 3 - Collaboration Methods*

Collaboration workflows:

options.text: The centralized workflow uses a central repository with a single branch
options.explanation: True. Everyone works on the single main branch of the central repo.

options.text: The feature-branch workflow emphasizes short-lived branches
options.explanation: False. Feature branches can live for a long time; short-lived branches are the trunk-based emphasis.

options.text: Trunk-based development emphasizes frequent change integrations to the main branch
options.explanation: True. Trunk-based development integrates small changes to main very often.

options.text: All statements are incorrect
options.explanation: False. a and c are correct.

questions.explanation: Centralized: everyone commits to one branch in a central repo. Feature branch: each feature gets its own branch, merged via pull request. Trunk-based: small, frequent merges to main.

questions.stem:
*Week 4 - Software Design*

[Week 3 review] Choose the correct statements:

options.text: Git commit can't be undone
options.explanation: False. Commits can be undone with `git revert` or `git reset`.

options.text: A commit can have more than two parents
options.explanation: True. An octopus merge of several branches has more than two parents.

options.text: Merge conflict always happens if the same file was changed in two different branches
options.explanation: False. Conflicts happen only when the same lines (or nearby lines) change differently.

options.text: Git branching is usually slow
options.explanation: False. A branch is just a pointer, so branching is fast and cheap.

options.text: Git cloning gives you all versions of the project
options.explanation: True. A clone copies the full repository with its whole history.

options.text: It is not possible to have a centralized repository in Git
options.explanation: False. A central repo is a common convention in Git.

questions.explanation: Review of Week 3: commits, merging, branching and cloning.

options.text: Code snippet 1
options.explanation: Wrong. Snippet 1 creates its own `Driver` with `new`, so it is tightly coupled (the field name does not make it DI).

options.text: Code snippet 2
options.explanation: Correct. Snippet 2 receives the `Driver` through its constructor (constructor injection).

options.text: Both of them
options.explanation: Wrong. Snippet 1 is not DI.

options.text: None of them
options.explanation: Wrong. Snippet 2 is DI.

questions.explanation: In dependency injection the object does not create its dependencies; they are passed in from outside.

questions.stem:
*Week 4 - Software Design*

Choose the correct statement about dependency injection (DI):

options.text: DI is compulsory in Java applications
options.explanation: False. DI is a design technique, not required by Java.

options.text: Dependencies can be defined via constructor arguments
options.explanation: True. Constructor injection is the main variant.

options.text: DI means object controls the creation of its dependencies
options.explanation: False. It is the opposite: control of creation is inverted to the container.

options.text: DI was invented in Hollywood
options.explanation: False. "Hollywood principle" ("don't call us, we'll call you") is only a nickname for IoC.

options.text: Dependencies can't be defined via fields
options.explanation: False. Field injection with `@Autowired` exists.

options.text: DI makes the code more tightly coupled
options.explanation: False. DI makes code loosely coupled and easier to test.

questions.explanation: DI is a form of Inversion of Control: a container (e.g. Spring) creates dependencies and injects them through the constructor, setters or fields.

questions.stem:
*Week 4 - Software Design*

Which is the preferred DI variant, and why?
questions.modelAnswer:
Constructor injection. All required dependencies must be provided (not null) when the object is created, so the object is always valid.
The fields can be `final`, giving immutable objects, and the class can be created in a unit test with mocks without the DI container.
A long constructor argument list also exposes a code smell (too many responsibilities). Field injection hides dependencies, couples the class to the container and makes it too easy to add dependencies. Setter injection fits only optional dependencies (or breaking a circular dependency).
questions.explanation: The slides compare constructor, setter and field injection. Constructor injection is preferred for required dependencies.

questions.stem:
*Week 4 - Software Design*

Software architecture: select all the incorrect statements

options.text: Monolithic architecture should not be used at all
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: A monolith is simple and fine for small apps and teams.

options.text: Microservices promote tight coupling of components
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Microservices aim for loose coupling between independent services.

options.text: REST is based on microservices architecture
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: REST is an architectural style for web APIs, independent of microservices.

options.text: Microservices architecture makes it more difficult to scale parts of an application individually
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Microservices make it easier to scale one service on its own.

questions.explanation: All four statements are incorrect.

questions.stem:
*Week 4 - Software Design*

Choose the correct statements about HTTP methods:

options.text: A safe method is not necessarily idempotent
options.explanation: False. A safe method changes nothing, so repeating it is always idempotent.

options.text: An unsafe method is not idempotent
options.explanation: False. PUT and DELETE are unsafe but idempotent.

options.text: POST is idempotent, meaning multiple identical POST requests will always have the same effect
options.explanation: False. POST is not idempotent; each POST may create a new resource.

options.text: GET is intended only for retrieving data
options.explanation: True. GET only reads data.

questions.explanation: Safe = does not change server state (GET, HEAD). Idempotent = repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once (GET, PUT, DELETE). Every safe method is idempotent.

questions.stem:
*Week 4 - Software Design*

Choose the correct statement about HTTP status codes:

options.text: 200 means everything is alright
options.explanation: True. 200 OK.

options.text: 404 means resource has been found
options.explanation: False. 404 means Not Found.

options.text: 201 does not mean anything
options.explanation: False. 201 means Created (e.g. after a successful POST).

options.text: 403 means user is not authenticated
options.explanation: False. 403 means Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed); 401 means not authenticated.

options.text: We must not return any HTTP codes from our APIs
options.explanation: False. APIs should always return proper status codes.

questions.explanation: REST APIs should return meaningful status codes: 2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

questions.stem:
*Week 4 - Software Design*

Best practices for REST API:

options.text: Should be implemented in Java
options.explanation: False. REST is language independent.

options.text: Should use nouns for resources in API paths
options.explanation: True. Paths name resources (`/books`), and HTTP methods give the action.

options.text: Should follow a standard which is strictly enforced
options.explanation: False. REST is a style with conventions, not a strictly enforced standard.

options.text: Should show major.minor.patch version on public API paths
options.explanation: False. Public paths show only the major version (e.g. `/v1/`).

questions.explanation: REST is an architectural style with conventions such as noun resources (`/books/1`) and HTTP verbs for actions.

questions.stem:
*Week 5 - Persistence*

[Week 4 Review] 1) You have used the command "mvnw" in the previous lab. What is it? 2) What is the purpose of the pom.xml file in your Spring Boot project?
questions.modelAnswer:
1) `mvnw` is the Maven Wrapper: a script in the project that downloads and runs a fixed Maven version, so you can build without installing Maven yourself (e.g. `./mvnw spring-boot:run`).
2) `pom.xml` (Project Object Model) is Maven's build file. It declares the project's details, its dependencies (e.g. Spring Boot starters), plugins and build settings.
questions.explanation: Both are part of building a Spring Boot project with Maven.

questions.stem:
*Week 5 - Persistence*

Regarding JDBC: select all correct statements

options.text: You only need to know Java when using JDBC
options.explanation: False. You also need SQL.

options.text: We have to write SQL in JDBC
options.explanation: True. Queries are SQL strings sent through JDBC.

options.text: JDBC hides DB-specific implementation details
options.explanation: True. A vendor driver implements the JDBC interfaces, so your code does not depend on the DB's protocol.

options.text: None are correct
options.explanation: False. b and c are correct.

questions.explanation: JDBC is a low-level Java API: you write the SQL yourself, and the driver hides the DB-specific details.

questions.stem:
*Week 5 - Persistence*

Object Relational Mapping: select all correct statements

options.text: Java class name can be mapped to objects
options.explanation: False. A class maps to a table, not to objects.

options.text: Java field names can be mapped to DB columns
options.explanation: True. Each field maps to a column.

options.text: Java object can be mapped to a DB row
options.explanation: True. Each object instance maps to a row.

options.text: None are correct
options.explanation: False. b and c are correct.

questions.explanation: ORM maps class to table, field to column, and object to row.

questions.stem:
*Week 5 - Persistence*

Problems with ORM:

options.text: Too much JDBC boilerplate code
options.explanation: False. Removing boilerplate is a benefit of ORM.

options.text: Confusing code
options.explanation: True. Annotations and generated queries hide what happens, which can confuse.

options.text: Can't do many-to-many mapping
options.explanation: False. ORM supports many-to-many (`@ManyToMany`).

options.text: Might not be very performant
options.explanation: True. Generated SQL can be slow (e.g. N+1 queries).

questions.explanation: ORM removes JDBC boilerplate, but its hidden queries can be confusing and slow.

questions.stem:
*Week 5 - Persistence*

Relationship mapping: select all correct statements

options.text: @Entity: to map a field to a column
options.explanation: False. `@Entity` maps a class to a table; `@Column` maps a field.

options.text: JPA assumes composition by default
options.explanation: False. JPA assumes aggregation by default.

options.text: Aggregation: child entity can't exist without parent
options.explanation: False. That describes composition; in aggregation the child can exist alone.

options.text: @ManyToMany produces a junction table
options.explanation: True. A many-to-many needs a join (junction) table.

questions.explanation: `@Entity` maps a class to a table. JPA assumes aggregation by default. Composition means the child cannot exist without its parent.

options.text: "mappedBy": indicate that the foreign key for the relationship is in the class User
options.explanation: False. `mappedBy` means the foreign key is in the other class (`UserProfile`).

options.text: "CascadeType.ALL": all persistence operations will not be propagated to relating entities
options.explanation: False. `CascadeType.ALL` propagates all operations (persist, remove, ...).

options.text: "@JoinColumn": specify the foreign key name
options.explanation: True. `@JoinColumn(name = "user_id")` names the foreign key column.

options.text: None of the above are correct
options.explanation: False. c is correct.

questions.explanation: `UserProfile` owns the relationship: its table has the `user_id` foreign key. `User` is the inverse side (`mappedBy`).

options.text: This code implements an aggregation
options.explanation: False. In aggregation the child would survive alone; here it does not.

options.text: This code implements a composition
options.explanation: True. Reviews cannot exist without their book: composition.

options.text: This code implements neither
options.explanation: False. It is a composition.

options.text: If a review is removed from the "reviews" list, it does not get deleted from DB
options.explanation: False. `orphanRemoval = true` deletes a review removed from the list.

questions.explanation: `orphanRemoval = true` plus `CascadeType.ALL` make each review's life depend on its book.

options.text: You will have to provide implementation for methods such as findAll(), findByTitle(), etc.
options.explanation: False. CRUD methods come from `CrudRepository`; `findByTitle` is derived from its name.

options.text: You need to implement the BookRepository interface for your code to work
options.explanation: False. You only declare the interface.

options.text: BookRepository will be implemented by Spring automatically
options.explanation: True. Spring creates the implementation automatically.

options.text: None of these options are correct
options.explanation: False. c is correct.

questions.explanation: Spring Data JPA generates the repository implementation at runtime, including derived queries such as `findByTitle`.

questions.stem:
*Week 5 - Persistence*

Non-relational databases: select all correct statements

options.text: NoSQL databases must use data tables with columns and rows
options.explanation: False. Tables with rows and columns are the relational model.

options.text: Data can be stored in the form of documents
options.explanation: True. Document stores (e.g. MongoDB) store JSON-like documents.

options.text: Can achieve improved scalability
options.explanation: True. They scale horizontally across many servers.

options.text: Not suitable for big data applications
options.explanation: False. They are widely used for big data.

questions.explanation: NoSQL databases store documents, key-values, wide columns or graphs, and scale out well.

questions.stem:
*Week 5 - Persistence*

Vector databases and embeddings: select all correct statements

options.text: Embeddings are vector representations of data
options.explanation: True. An embedding is a numeric vector that captures meaning.

options.text: SQL databases cannot store embeddings
options.explanation: False. SQL databases can store them (e.g. PostgreSQL with pgvector).

options.text: Vector databases enable fast similarity searches
options.explanation: True. They are built for fast similarity search.

options.text: Public LLM services such as OpenAI GPT-4 should have information about all your data and products
options.explanation: False. Public LLMs do not know your private data, which is why RAG is used.

questions.explanation: Embeddings turn data into vectors; vector databases index them for fast nearest-neighbour search, e.g. for RAG.

questions.stem:
*Week 6 - Sprint Planning and Execution*

[Week 5 review] Choose all the correct statements:

options.text: In Java apps, we can access the database via JDBC or JPA
options.explanation: True. Both are standard ways to reach a DB from Java.

options.text: You can't use SQL statements when using JPA
options.explanation: False. JPA allows native SQL queries (and JPQL).

options.text: Under the hood, JPA implementations can use JDBC to access the database
options.explanation: True. JPA providers such as Hibernate use JDBC underneath.

options.text: @Entity annotation is to map a Java class to a column
options.explanation: False. `@Entity` maps a class to a table.

options.text: "orphanRemoval = true": removing a child will remove its parent as well
options.explanation: False. It deletes the orphaned child, not the parent.

options.text: Spring Data JPA generates code to implement your repositories automatically
options.explanation: True. Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations.

options.text: A transaction does not have to be atomic
options.explanation: False. Transactions must be atomic (ACID).

options.text: It is best to store vector embeddings in SQL databases
options.explanation: False. Vector databases are built for embeddings and similarity search.

questions.explanation: Review of Week 5: JDBC, JPA, entities, transactions and vector databases.

questions.stem:
*Week 6 - Sprint Planning and Execution*

[Review] In a concise manner, explain how does Spring work?
questions.modelAnswer:
Spring's core is an IoC (Inversion of Control) container, the application context. It scans the classpath for components (`@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@RestController`...), creates them as beans and manages their lifecycle.
It then wires beans together by dependency injection (auto-wiring), so classes receive their dependencies instead of creating them: "Don't call us, we'll call you". Spring Boot adds auto-configuration on top.
questions.explanation: Spring is built on Inversion of Control and dependency injection.

questions.stem:
*Week 6 - Sprint Planning and Execution*

Backlog refinement: select all incorrect statements

options.text: During backlog refinement, we can remove some user stories
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: Outdated or unneeded stories can be removed.

options.text: During backlog refinement, acceptance criteria should be added or clarified for each item.
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: Adding and clarifying acceptance criteria is a core refinement task.

options.text: Backlog refinement takes place only at the start of each sprint.
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Refinement happens throughout the sprint, not only at the start.

options.text: Backlog refinement is solely for documentation purposes.
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: It prepares items (split, estimate, clarify) for sprint planning, not just documents them.

questions.explanation: The question asks for the incorrect statements. Refinement is ongoing work that keeps the backlog ready for planning.

questions.stem:
*Week 6 - Sprint Planning and Execution*

Definition of ready: select all correct statements

options.text: A backlog item is considered ready when it is fully implemented and demonstrated to users.
options.explanation: False. That describes "done", not "ready".

options.text: The definition of ready requires that acceptance criteria for backlog items are testable.
options.explanation: True. Testable acceptance criteria are part of ready.

options.text: Backlog items do not need to be estimated before being considered ready.
options.explanation: False. Ready items must be estimated.

options.text: Items large enough to span a few sprints can still meet the definition of ready.
options.explanation: False. Ready items must fit within one sprint.

questions.explanation: "Ready" means an item is clear, testable, estimated and small enough to finish within one sprint.

questions.stem:
*Week 6 - Sprint Planning and Execution*

Sprint planning and execution: select all correct statements

options.text: The sprint goal should be decided by the product owner.
options.explanation: False. The whole Scrum team agrees the sprint goal.

options.text: Decomposition of backlog items into executable technical tasks is part of sprint planning.
options.explanation: True. Items are split into technical tasks in sprint planning.

options.explanation: True. Items can be re-estimated as understanding improves.

options.text: Only code development activities are done during sprint execution.
options.explanation: False. Execution also includes testing, reviews, refinement and daily scrums.

questions.stem:
*Week 9 - Security*

[Review] Choose all the incorrect statements:

options.text: The sprint goal should be decided by the user.
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: The Scrum team sets the sprint goal.

options.text: We should only decompose backlog items into executable technical tasks during sprint retrospective.
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Decomposition happens in sprint planning; the retrospective improves the process.

options.text: Re-estimation of any backlog items is not allowed during backlog refinement.
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Re-estimation is allowed in refinement.

options.text: During the sprint, we can perform estimation for some tasks.
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: New or changed tasks can be estimated during the sprint.

options.text: A user story is considered ready when it is added into the backlog.
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Ready requires meeting the definition of ready (clear, testable, estimated, small).

options.text: During backlog refinement, we can add new user stories.
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: New stories can be added during refinement.

questions.explanation: The question asks for the incorrect statements. Review of Week 6: sprint planning, refinement and definition of ready.

questions.stem:
*Week 9 - Security*

About trust - select all the correct statements:

options.text: We should trust the data sent from our users
options.explanation: False. User input must always be validated.

options.text: We can completely trust the network between our server and the clients
options.explanation: False. The network can be sniffed or tampered with; use HTTPS.

options.text: We should not use any external dependencies as we don't trust them :(
options.explanation: False. External dependencies are fine if vetted and kept updated.

options.text: None are correct
options.explanation: True. a, b and c are all wrong.

questions.explanation: Zero trust: validate all input, secure the network (HTTPS), and vet dependencies instead of banning them.

questions.stem:
*Week 9 - Security*

Input validation: choose the correct statements

options.text: Mixing code and data in your software is a good practice
options.explanation: False. Mixing code and data leads to injection attacks (e.g. SQL injection).

options.text: Whitelisting rejects inputs containing known dangerous values
options.explanation: False. That is blacklisting; whitelisting accepts only known-good values.

options.text: Jakarta Bean Validation API can define constraints on fields of a class via Java annotations
options.explanation: True. E.g. `@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Email` on fields.

options.text: If the user input is not valid, your API should return a 404 HTTP status
options.explanation: False. Invalid input returns 400 Bad Request; 404 means not found.

options.text: @Valid can be used to check the arguments provided to controller's methods
options.explanation: True. `@Valid` on a controller parameter triggers validation.

questions.explanation: Validate input with allow-lists and Bean Validation annotations; reject bad input with 400.

questions.stem:
*Week 9 - Security*

Authentication and authorization - choose the incorrect statements:

options.text: Authorization is to determine who you want
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Authorization decides what you can do.

options.text: Authentication is to determine what you can do
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Authentication decides who you are.

options.text: Basic HTTP authentication is secure with bcrypt password hashing
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Basic auth only Base64-encodes credentials on every request; it needs HTTPS. Bcrypt only protects stored passwords.

options.text: In hashing, it is very hard to produce an output
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Hashing is easy to compute; it is hard to reverse.

options.text: Encryption is to convert cipher text into plain text
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Encryption turns plain text into cipher text; decryption does the reverse.

questions.explanation: The question asks for the incorrect statements, and all five are incorrect.

questions.stem:
*Week 9 - Security*

Briefly explain why in hashing, the salt is not stored as a secret?
questions.modelAnswer:
The salt's job is only to make each hash unique: the same password with different salts gives different hashes, so precomputed lookup (rainbow) tables don't work. It doesn't need to be secret for that.
It is unique per user and stored with the hashed password, because the server needs it to re-hash the login password and compare. Security comes from the slow hash (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2), not from hiding the salt.
questions.explanation: A salt is a random value added to each password before hashing.

questions.stem:
*Week 9 - Security*

A logged-in user tries to perform an unauthorized action:

options.text: A status code of 401 should be returned
options.explanation: False. 401 Unauthorized means not authenticated (not logged in).

options.text: A status code of 400 should be returned
options.explanation: False. 400 Bad Request means invalid input.

options.text: A status code of 403 should be returned
options.explanation: True. 403 Forbidden: logged in but no permission.

options.text: No status code should be returned
options.explanation: False. APIs must always return a status code.

questions.explanation: The user is authenticated but not allowed, so the answer is 403 Forbidden.

options.text: The code does not allow clients to do basic authentication by sending username/password in the HTTP header
options.explanation: False. `httpBasic()` enables basic authentication.

options.text: You can post to the URL "/books/1" if authenticated
options.explanation: False. POST is only allowed on `/books`, not `/books/1`.

options.text: You can update a book via the URL "/books/1" if authenticated
options.explanation: True. PUT on `/books/*` matches `/books/1` for authenticated users.

options.text: All options are incorrect
options.explanation: False. c is correct.

questions.explanation: Each `requestMatchers` rule pairs an HTTP method with a URL pattern.

questions.stem:
*Week 9 - Security*

[JWT vs. Basic Auth] Choose all the correct statements:

options.text: JWTs have built-in expiration capabilities
options.explanation: True. The `exp` claim sets the expiry.

options.text: JWTs are completely secure without HTTPS
options.explanation: False. A stolen token can be replayed, so HTTPS is still needed.

options.text: Basic authentication requires sending username/password with every single request to the server
options.explanation: True. Basic auth is stateless and sends credentials every time.

options.text: JWTs are only used for authentication, not for authorization
options.explanation: False. JWT claims (e.g. roles) are also used for authorization.

options.text: JWTs are always encrypted, so their contents cannot be read by anyone
options.explanation: False. JWTs are signed, not encrypted; the Base64url payload is readable.

questions.explanation: A JWT is a signed token with claims; Basic Auth sends the credentials on every request.

questions.stem:
*Week 9 - Security*

[Cors] Select all the correct statements:

options.text: Two URLs with different ports are considered different origins.
options.explanation: True. A different port means a different origin.

options.text: The same-origin policy allows scripts from http://myapp.com to access resources from https://myapp.com
options.explanation: False. http and https are different schemes, so different origins.

options.text: CORS is automatically enabled in all Spring Boot applications by default.
options.explanation: False. CORS must be configured in Spring (e.g. `@CrossOrigin` or a CORS config).

options.text: If a backend API is running at http://localhost:8080 and the frontend is at http://localhost, requests from the frontend to the backend are considered same-origin.
options.explanation: False. Port 80 vs 8080 makes them different origins.

questions.explanation: Origin = scheme + host + port; all three must match to be same-origin.

questions.stem:
*Week 10 - Software Testing*

[Week 9 Review] Select all the incorrect statements:

options.text: Attackers can't see your text password sent in the HTTP header if it's encoded in Base64
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Base64 is an encoding, decoded by anyone.

options.text: It is a must to store plaintext passwords in database
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Store only salted, slow hashes.

options.text: A status code of 403 should be returned when resource is not found
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Not found is 404; 403 is forbidden.

options.text: Authorization is to determine the permissions of users
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: Authorization decides what a user may do.

options.text: Whitelisting rejects inputs containing known dangerous values
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Whitelisting accepts only known-good values.

options.text: It is better to implement your own algorithm for password hashing
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Use well-tested libraries (bcrypt, argon2); never roll your own crypto.

options.text: JWTs can be signed using asymmetric signing algorithms
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: JWTs can be signed with RSA or ECDSA key pairs (e.g. RS256).

questions.explanation: The question asks for the incorrect statements. Review of Week 9 security.

questions.stem:
*Week 10 - Software Testing*

What's the purpose of software testing?

options.text: To uncover bugs
options.explanation: True. Testing finds defects.

options.text: To learn about the software
options.explanation: True. Tests show how the software actually behaves.

options.text: To clarify user stories
options.explanation: True. Acceptance tests make user stories concrete.

options.text: To verify contracts
options.explanation: True. Tests check that components meet their contracts (specs, interfaces).

options.text: To assess quality of the software
options.explanation: True. Test results give a measure of quality.

questions.explanation: All five options are purposes of testing given in the course.

questions.stem:
*Week 10 - Software Testing*

Which of the following is not a good software testing approach?

options.text: Try to devise all test cases
options.explanation: True. Testing every case is infeasible; choose representative cases.

options.text: Select random parts of the code to test as software behavior is not predictable
options.explanation: True. Tests should be designed systematically, not picked at random.

options.text: Wait for the software to fail in production, then perform some tests
options.explanation: True. Testing must happen before production.

options.text: Conduct tests only when development is done
options.explanation: True. Testing should start early and run continuously.

options.text: Try to find only cases in which the code would work well
options.explanation: True. Tests should try to make the code fail.

questions.explanation: All five are bad approaches. Good testing is systematic (partitions, boundaries), early and aimed at finding failures.

questions.stem:
*Week 10 - Software Testing*

Choose the correct statements about TDD, blackbox/whitebox, etc.:

options.text: In TDD, we write the application code first
options.explanation: False. TDD writes the test first.

options.text: In blackbox testing, we look at the code to design test cases
options.explanation: False. Black-box testing does not look at the code.

options.text: In whitebox testing, we only look at the input to the application to be tested
options.explanation: False. White-box testing looks at the code's structure.

options.text: Length of valid input is from 40 to 100 characters: we can have 3 partitions of the input space
options.explanation: True. Partitions: under 40, 40-100, over 100.

options.text: Boundary values are useful because they can make the app fails
options.explanation: True. Bugs cluster at boundaries (e.g. 39, 40, 100, 101).

questions.explanation: Black-box tests come from the spec; white-box tests come from the code.

options.text: If a test uses "a = True", it can achieve 100% branch coverage
options.explanation: False. `a = true` runs every statement but misses the false branch.

options.text: If a test uses "a = False", it can achieve 100% path coverage
options.explanation: False. `a = false` covers one path only (and divides by zero).

options.text: It is not possible to achieve 100% branch coverage in this case
options.explanation: False. Two tests (true and false) give 100% branch coverage.

options.text: It is possible to achieve 100% statement coverage in this case
options.explanation: True. `a = true` alone runs every statement.

questions.explanation: Statement coverage counts lines run; branch coverage needs both outcomes of `if (a)`; path coverage needs every path.

questions.stem:
*Week 10 - Software Testing*

Coverage: choose the correct statements

options.text: Code coverage is the most important measure in software testing
options.explanation: False. Coverage is not an adequacy criterion.

options.text: Assertion-free testing is a good software testing approach
options.explanation: False. Tests without assertions never fail, so they inflate coverage without checking anything.

options.text: 100% code coverage does not ensure that all customer requirements are met
options.explanation: True. Covered code can still be wrong, and missing features have no code to cover.

options.text: We should not measure code coverage at all
options.explanation: False. Coverage is useful for finding untested code.

questions.explanation: Coverage shows what code ran, not whether the behaviour is right.

questions.stem:
*Week 10 - Software Testing*

Provide three (3) good reasons for using code coverage measures?
questions.modelAnswer:
1) Identifies untested code.
2) Shows places where testing is inadequate, to guide which new test cases to write.
3) Gives an objective, automatically computed measure (e.g. with JaCoCo) to track test progress over time and spot unreachable or dead code.
questions.explanation: Coverage is a tool to find gaps in testing, not a goal in itself.
questions.source: given + from course: 10-Software Testing.pdf + own answer

options.text: The test will fail if bookService.addBook() returns null
options.explanation: True. `assertNotNull(savedBook)` fails on null.

options.text: The actual JPA repository's findByTitle method was called during the test
options.explanation: False. Only the mock is called; the real repository is never used.

options.text: The mock is configured to return an empty list when findByTitle is called with any string
options.explanation: True. `any(String.class)` matches any title, and the stub returns an empty list.

options.text: The "when(books.save(any(Book.class))).thenReturn(book)" statement ensures that when save() is called with any Book object, it will return the exact same book object that was passed to addBook()
options.explanation: False. It always returns the fixed `book` variable, whatever Book is passed to `save()`.

questions.explanation: `@Mock` creates a fake repository and `@InjectMocks` puts it into the service; `when(...).thenReturn(...)` stubs its answers.

questions.stem:
*Week 10 - Software Testing*

Testing practices: choose the correct statements

options.text: You need immediate feedback from unit tests
options.explanation: True. Fast unit tests give quick feedback on each change.

options.text: Unit tests should validate multiple software components at the same time
options.explanation: False. A unit test isolates one component.

options.text: Mocking can be used in unit tests
options.explanation: True. Mocks replace dependencies to isolate the unit.

options.text: Integration tests usually run faster than unit tests
options.explanation: False. Integration tests are slower (DB, network, more code).

options.text: Regression testing: we can run previously passed integration tests
options.explanation: True. Regression testing reruns earlier passing tests to catch new breakage.

questions.explanation: Unit tests check one unit in isolation and run fast; integration tests check units together and run slower.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

[Week 10 Review] Select all the correct statements:

options.text: A good testing approach is to cover all possible inputs from users
options.explanation: False. Testing all inputs is infeasible.

options.text: Unit testing only tests one line of code at a time
options.explanation: False. A unit is a method or class, not a line.

options.text: Integration tests might need mocking
options.explanation: True. External services (e.g. a payment API) may still be mocked in integration tests.

options.text: Good code coverage number ensures high quality test cases
options.explanation: False. Coverage says nothing about assertion quality.

options.text: Boundary value analysis is used together with input space partitioning to find good test cases
options.explanation: True. Partition the input space, then test the partition boundaries.

options.text: "when(bookRepository.findById(bookId)).thenReturn(Optional.of(existingBook));" -> this line of code calls the "findById" method in the actual JPA repository
options.explanation: False. `when()` stubs the mock; the real repository is not called.

questions.explanation: Review of Week 10 testing.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

Which are some good reasons to do code review?

options.text: Insurance against author's disappearance
options.explanation: True. Reviewers know the code if the author leaves.

options.text: Improve accountability
options.explanation: True. Authors write more carefully when others will read their code.

options.text: Force code documentation
options.explanation: True. Code must be understandable to the reviewer, so it gets documented.

options.text: Improve development speed
options.explanation: True. Catching defects early saves time later.

questions.explanation: All four are benefits of code review given in the course.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

Which code needs review?

options.text: Code that is below a triviality threshold
options.explanation: False. Trivial changes can skip review.

options.text: Highly abstract algorithms
options.explanation: True. Complex, abstract code is hard to get right.

options.text: Code written by experienced developers
options.explanation: True. Experts make mistakes too.

options.text: Buggy code
options.explanation: True. Buggy areas need extra review.

questions.explanation: Everything above a triviality threshold should be reviewed, whoever wrote it.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

Technical debts:

options.text: Reduce time when removing existing features
options.explanation: False. Debt makes every change, removals included, slower.

options.text: Can be caused by management deadlines
options.explanation: True. Deadline pressure leads to shortcuts.

options.text: Incur more time to understand current implementation
options.explanation: True. Messy code takes longer to understand.

options.text: Are the extra effort that it takes to add new features
options.explanation: False. Debt is the extra effort caused by poor code, not the normal effort of adding features.

questions.explanation: Technical debt is the extra future cost caused by quick-and-dirty, not-quite-right code.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

When should you do refactoring:

options.text: When the code is well-structured
options.explanation: False. Well-structured code does not need refactoring.

options.text: When the code has duplication
options.explanation: True. Duplication is a classic smell.

options.text: When you are trying to fix bugs
options.explanation: True. Making code clearer helps find and fix the bug.

options.text: After a code review session
options.explanation: True. Reviews reveal smells to fix.

options.text: When adding new features and the current code is messy
options.explanation: True. Clean up first, then add the feature.

options.text: When we have no test cases
options.explanation: False. Write tests first; refactoring without tests is risky.

questions.explanation: Refactor when code smells, as part of daily work, with tests as a safety net.

options.text: Remove the assignment to parameter
options.explanation: True. "Remove assignments to parameters" is the named refactoring.

options.text: No need refactoring; the code already looks good
options.explanation: False. Reassigning `inputVal` is a smell.

options.text: Use "final" keywords on parameters
options.explanation: True. `final` parameters make the compiler block reassignment.

options.text: Do not use parameters
options.explanation: False. The method needs its inputs; only the reassignment is the problem.

questions.explanation: The smell is assignment to a parameter. Use a local variable (`int result = inputVal;`) and change `result` instead.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

What could be considered a code smell?

options.text: A method mostly uses data from its own class
options.explanation: False. That is normal; feature envy is using another class's data.

options.text: Method parameter is reassigned in the method's body
options.explanation: True. Assignment to a parameter.

options.text: try {...} catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException("e");}
options.explanation: True. Catching a generic `Exception` and rethrowing with a useless message hides the real error.

options.text: A long Java method
options.explanation: True. Long method.

options.text: Syntax errors
options.explanation: False. Syntax errors are compile errors, not smells.

questions.explanation: A code smell is a design weakness that slows development, not a bug.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

Select all the benefits of pair programming:

options.text: Knowledge sharing
options.explanation: True. Both developers learn the code and each other's skills.

options.text: Keeping focus
options.explanation: True. A partner keeps you on task.

options.text: Code review on the go
options.explanation: True. The navigator reviews each line as it is written.

options.text: Individual code ownership
options.explanation: False. Pairing builds collective, not individual, ownership.

options.text: Fast for onboarding new members
options.explanation: True. New members learn quickly by pairing.

options.text: Improve design quality
options.explanation: True. Two people discuss design choices.

questions.explanation: Pairing spreads knowledge and reviews code as it is written.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

Pairing styles:

options.text: Expert-novice should not be used in driver-navigator pairing
options.explanation: False. Expert-novice is a common driver-navigator pairing.

options.text: It is not possible to do novice-novice pairing
options.explanation: False. Novice-novice pairing is possible, though it needs support.

options.text: In driver-navigator pairing, the navigator is in charge of tactical thinking
options.explanation: False. The driver handles tactics; the navigator thinks strategically.

options.text: Strong-style pairing involves an expert and a novice
options.explanation: True. "For an idea to go into the computer, it must go through someone else's hands."

options.text: Red-Green-Refactor: red and green refer to failing and passing tests, respectively
options.explanation: True. Red = failing test, green = passing test (ping-pong / TDD).

questions.explanation: Driver = types, tactical; navigator = reviews, strategic. Strong style: the expert navigates and the novice drives.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

Pairing - what you should do:

options.text: Choose a user story and start programming right away
options.explanation: False. Plan before coding.

options.text: Must finish a user story in a pairing session
options.explanation: False. A story can span sessions.

options.text: Should only do pairing face to face
options.explanation: False. Remote pairing works with screen sharing.

options.text: Need to do some planning before the pairing session
options.explanation: True. Agree the goal and approach first.

questions.explanation: Plan the session first: goal, tasks, roles, breaks.

questions.stem:
*Week 11 - Code Review, Refactoring and Pair Programming*

Pairing - what you should not do:

options.text: Reply to emails during the session
options.explanation: True. Should not do: It breaks focus.

options.text: Stop your partner right away when he makes a mistake
options.explanation: True. Should not do: Wait a few seconds; the driver may spot it.

options.text: Should leave room for others to think
options.explanation: False. Leaving room to think is good practice.

options.text: Snatch the keyboard whenever you can
options.explanation: True. Should not do: Switch roles respectfully.

questions.explanation: The question asks for bad pairing behaviour.

questions.stem:
*Week 12 - Deployment*

Computing infrastructure:

options.text: All containers running on the same host share the host OS kernel
options.explanation: True. Containers are isolated processes on the shared host kernel.

options.text: VMs provide better security and isolation capability compared to containers
options.explanation: True. Each VM has its own kernel, so isolation is stronger.

options.text: In Platform as a Service (PaaS), users manage the operating system and virtualization layers
options.explanation: False. In PaaS the provider manages the OS and virtualisation; users manage apps and data (that is IaaS).

options.text: Container images are typically much larger in size (GB) compared to VM images (MB)
options.explanation: False. It is the other way round: container images are MBs, VM images GBs.

questions.explanation: VMs virtualise hardware and each runs a full guest OS. Containers virtualise the OS and share the host kernel.

questions.stem:
*Week 12 - Deployment*

Cloud services:

options.text: On-premises: less control over your infrastructure
options.explanation: False. On-premises gives more control.

options.text: On-premises: may have issues of resource under-utilization
options.explanation: True. Hardware bought for peak load sits idle at other times.

options.text: Cloud-based: issues of vendor lock-in
options.explanation: True. Provider-specific services make moving away hard.

options.text: Cloud-based: need to spend much capital upfront
options.explanation: False. Cloud is pay-as-you-go (operating cost); upfront capital is the on-premises problem.

questions.explanation: On-premises gives full control but needs upfront hardware; cloud is pay-as-you-go but ties you to a provider.

questions.stem:
*Week 12 - Deployment*

Software packaging methods: select all the incorrect statements

options.text: In a multi-stage Docker build, the runtime stage typically uses the full JDK to run the application
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: The runtime stage uses a small JRE image; the JDK is only in the build stage.

options.text: A Dockerfile using single-stage build includes all build tools, compilers, and dependencies in the final image
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: A single-stage image keeps every build tool, so it is large.

options.text: Docker Compose can only be used to run applications locally
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: Compose can also run multi-container apps on servers.

options.text: When using containerized applications, developers still need to ensure the host machine has the right JVM
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: The image already contains the JVM; the host only needs a container runtime.

questions.explanation: The question asks for the incorrect statements. Containers package the app with its runtime; multi-stage builds keep the final image small.

questions.stem:
*Week 12 - Deployment*

Continuous X:

options.text: Staging environment incurs no additional cost
options.explanation: False. Staging copies production infrastructure, so it costs money.

options.text: Production environment contains real customer data
options.explanation: True. Production serves real users and their data.

options.text: In continuous integration, we manually build and test software when there is a new commit
options.explanation: False. CI builds and tests automatically on each commit.

options.text: Continuous delivery does not deploy to production automatically
options.explanation: True. The production release needs a manual approval step.

questions.explanation: CI builds and tests every commit automatically. Continuous delivery keeps the software always releasable, with a manual approval to production. Continuous deployment releases automatically.

questions.stem:
*Week 12 - Deployment*

DevSecOps practices: select all the incorrect statements

options.text: SAST requires the software to be running before scanning can begin
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: SAST scans code without running it; DAST needs a running app.

options.text: SAST is used early in the SDLC, while DAST can only be used later in the development process
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: SAST runs on code early; DAST needs a running build, so it comes later.

options.text: DAST is a white-box testing approach that requires access to source code
options.explanation: True. Incorrect statement: DAST is black-box testing and needs no source code.

options.text: SAST might produce many false positives
options.explanation: False. Correct statement: Static analysis without runtime context often flags false positives.

questions.explanation: The question asks for the incorrect statements. SAST (static) scans source code without running it; DAST (dynamic) attacks the running app from outside.
